title: Eleven Seconds
passages:
The barge's smudge was gone from the slate's horizon, swallowed by rain and the dark water east of the Marrow. Wren stayed at the winch. The drum sat cold, the spliced line coiled neat as a sleeping snake, and the wheelhouse speaker hissed with Salas's ghost-call on the backup channel — *keep going... tell the kid* — but the sound that wouldn't leave her was the way he'd said her name. Not *reader* or *tech* or *hey you*. *Wren*. Like he knew her. Like she'd sworn him something.

Behind her, voices rose and fell in the galley. Sol and Rusk's parting words, Dey's jaw working, Nia's flat refusal to be moved. The storm was still hours out, but the air had that charge, the pressure drop that made your teeth ache. Wren's thumb hovered over the edit wheel. She'd rebuilt hundreds of lost hours. Divers came up hollow, their slates full of static and pressure spikes, and she stitched the gaps with deck audio, suit telemetry, the rhythm of a breath held too long. She'd never once run a build on herself.

Her slate was a cracked Gen-3 reader, salt-scored and held together with tape and stubbornness. She thumbed the build key, spoke the command: *"Self. Full spool. Last descent."* The machine didn't argue. It never did. A progress bar bloomed, green and patient, pulling telemetry from a dive her body had made and her mind had never seen.

Depth trace. Heart rate. Scrubber efficiency. Time stamps marching backward from the surface — *00:00, -00:12, -00:47* — into water she didn't remember. The suit's headlamp log showed a beam cutting green at twenty meters, thirty, thirty-five. Her own voice on the comms, calm and professional: *"Reader to surface. At pocket. Seal intact."* The build kept spooling.
